newsitem.title: CHILE: Escondida to fix cathode plant glitches.
newsitem.headline: Escondida to fix cathode plant glitches.

text.p: Escondida's cathodes plant has yet to fix a series of production glitches that have prevented it from reaching design capacity of 80,000 tonnes a year, company officials said.
But Escondida, majority owned by Australia's BHP, believes it can solve the problems in the next few months and hit 80,000 tonnes for fiscal 1998, which starts June 1, they said.

"We've still got a lot of fine-tuning to do so that the system works the way it's supposed to," an official told reporters during a visit to the plant. The plant produced about 50,000 tonnes of cathodes last year.
First of its kind in the world, the plant uses an ammonia-based solvent extraction system to make 99.99 percent pure copper cathodes from sulphides.

"The problem is that there's no history in this, no experience to go by. We're inventing the wheel here and that's what makes it difficult," said another official. All of them asked not to be identified.

Escondida officials have said in the past that the original problems were mainly of a mechancial nature and not associated with the plant's high-tech chemical processes. President Ken Pickering once called the problems "an embarrassment" but noted cathodes were still outside the company's core business of selling concentrates.
But the main impediment cited now by officials was in the extraction process, in which a solvent known as scaide 101 was leaving too much copper unseparated from waste.
"These chemical reactions are highly variable...and the main problem is in the extraction process, which is not releasing the copper as it should," said one official.
"We are working out this problem and approaching design capacity," he said. They reported no recent problems with the ammonia supply, which comes from the Chilean company Enaex.
The plant uses sulphide concentrates which, mixed with water to form slurry, wash down an underground pipeline stretching across the desert from the mine about 170 km away.

Most of the concentrates are strained in a huge tank and then loaded onto freighters at Escondida's pier at Puerto de Coloso, but part go to the cathodes factory. The finished cathodes, stacked up outside the plant, are then trucked to Antofagasta's port because Coloso is unequipped to load them.
